title: ArceKV: Towards Workload-driven LSM-compactions for Key-Value Store Under Dynamic Workloads
one_line: A RocksDB fork that removes LSM structural constraints (ElasticLSM) and picks compactions and write-stall thresholds online with a score-based cost model (Arce), to keep performance optimal while workloads shift.

repo.evidence: The paper's PVLDB Artifact Availability block (paper.txt p.1) names https://github.com/NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV; NTU-Siqiang-Group is the last author's (Siqiang Luo, NTU) group account, and the same org hosts MooseLSM and CAMAL which the paper cites as its own prior work (footnotes 3-4, p.8). The clone contains the real engine (db/dyncompactioner.cc, include/rocksdb/dyncompactionv4.h, db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc), not a stub.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - the ACM DL entry (10.14778/3796195.3796208) and the PVLDB PDF carry only an Artifact Availability statement, no reproducibility badge

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official (see repo.evidence) and it contains the actual system: ElasticLSM action enumeration at include/rocksdb/dyncompactionv4.h:81-157, the Arce cost model and effectiveness score at db/dyncompactioner.cc:7-62, Algorithm 1's parameter search at db/dyncompactioner.cc:199-235, the RocksDB compaction picker at db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:348-416, and the write-stall hook at db/column_family.cc:922-946. CAVEAT (does not flip the verdict but is the top reproduction risk): README.md:2 states the main branch is a TikTok-specific in-memory adaptation that 'does not represent a faithful implementation of ArceKV' (simplified write-stop, one SSTable per run, range-filter policy removed), and README.md:4 points to a 'dev' branch whose on-disk version is a separate re-implementation with different class names (kCompactionStyleArce / ArceCompactionController).

H2_no_root.evidence: Nothing in the build or run path needs privilege. The only in-code sudo is tools/dynamic_test_util.h:555-564 ('sudo -S fstrim -v /tmp' with a hard-coded password), which lives in a header excluded from the build (tools/CMakeLists.txt:17), is invoked through system() and only prints 'fail to trim' when it fails. README.md:27 ('sudo make install') is avoidable by running build/tools/arce_bench in-tree; README.md:53 ('sudo mount -t tmpfs') is avoidable by pointing --db_path at /dev/shm or at NVMe. No kernel module, eBPF, perf_event, KVM, or hugepage use; the sudo/sysctl/docker grep hits in repo_facts.json are all inherited upstream RocksDB CI (.circleci/config.yml, .github/actions/, build_tools/ubuntu20_image/Dockerfile) or doc prose about machine crash/reboot.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: CPU-only, single node, no GPU. Paper hardware (paper.txt p.8, section 5): i9-13900K, 128 GB RAM, 1 TB NVMe, 75 GiB cgroup memory cap - our 16-core Threadripper PRO 5955WX / 125 GiB / NVMe RAID is a superset except single-thread clock, and the 75 GiB cap is reproducible with the delegated cgroup-v2 memory controller. Workload I (Figure 9) is 245.76M ops, +74 GiB on a 40 GiB preload, so ~160-200 GB peak against ~250 GB free: fits at full scale, and the mechanism is scale-invariant because the count window is F/E = 2 MiB / 1024 B ~ 2048 updates regardless of dataset size. Figure 10(c)'s 16 foreground threads map exactly onto 16 cores. db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:404 caps output files at 100 GiB, which only matters for disk headroom, not fit.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: All dependencies are user-space installable: cmake 3.25 and gcc 12.2 are present (CMakeLists.txt:35 needs >=3.10); OpenMP is REQUIRED (CMakeLists.txt:47-48) and libgomp ships with gcc; TBB is linked unconditionally into every tool (tools/CMakeLists.txt:26, tools/arce_bench.cc:13) and gflags is on by default (CMakeLists.txt:134) - both from conda-forge; the grafite submodule is a hard dependency (table/block_based/filter_policy_internal.h:19 includes it unguarded, CMakeLists.txt:988-991) and .gitmodules uses an SSH URL, fixable with a git url.insteadOf rewrite. Data is entirely synthetic (24 B padded integer keys, 1000 B values - tools/arce_bench.cc:176-215, tools/dynamic_test_util.h:84-104); YCSB for Table 3 is public. No proprietary trace. The Table 2 / Workload I-III generator is absent from the repo and must be written (~100 lines), which is missing tooling, not unobtainable data.

reproduce.target: Figure 9 (left table), Workload I: the ArceKV-vs-1-Leveling throughput ratio on the point-lookup/update-only sub-workloads B (98% update; paper 10.60x vs 2.29x, i.e. ArceKV ~4.6x faster than RocksDB default leveling) and C (98% point; 3.08x vs 2.60x, i.e. ~1.2x). This supports the paper's core claim that one elastic policy wins at both ends of the read/write spectrum. Secondary smoke-test target: the repo's own README.md:67-86 table (ArceKV vs RocksDB at read_ratio 0.1-0.9), which tools/arce_bench.cc plus the tmp.py scraper produce directly.
reproduce.scale_down: 1/5 scale: 10 GiB sequential preload instead of 40 GiB and 8M ops per phase instead of 40.96M, keeping every mechanism-relevant knob at the paper's value (24 B keys, 1000 B values, 2 MB write buffer, Bloom 10 bpk, num_levels=4, simulation_iter=400) so the count window and the (M,c) search space are unchanged. DB on /home NVMe (not /dev/shm) so compaction I/O is real; RSS capped near 16 GiB via cgroup-v2 memory.max on the user slice to preserve the paper's memory:data ratio; single foreground thread and RocksDB default background jobs, matching section 5's 'one background compaction thread and one flush thread'.
reproduce.rationale: Not H: the harness that matches the paper (tools/dynamic_test.cc, with trace files, range lookups, continuous workloads, cache/thread/threshold sweeps) is commented out of the build at tools/CMakeLists.txt:17 and almost certainly no longer compiles - tools/dynamic_test_util.h:388 and :485 call FindBestMC unqualified while it is declared inside namespace DynamicLookForward (include/rocksdb/dynamic_lookforward.h:7-13) with no using directive and no ADL path. There is no workload generator, no plotting script and no run driver; the binary that does build (tools/arce_bench.cc) has an empty SCAN branch (:200-202), ignores UPDATE, and takes a single static read/write ratio (:26-27) so it cannot express a compound workload; grafite is an untested hard build dependency reachable only after an SSH->HTTPS rewrite; FAIL_ON_WARNINGS defaults ON (CMakeLists.txt:356) on a RocksDB 9.5 fork under gcc 12; and README.md:2 disclaims that main is a faithful ArceKV. Not L: the whole decision engine, picker and stall hook are present and legible, the build is plain CMake with conda-installable deps, the machine comfortably exceeds the paper's, all data is synthetic, and the repo ships its own quantitative result table (README.md:67-86) to validate the build against before touching paper numbers.

addons.name: oracle-free-workload-estimation
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing ArceKV's supplied next-window workload tuple and known change-point horizon with an online estimator (EWMA over completed count windows + CUSUM/Page-Hinkley change detection + an online estimate of the remaining horizon) costs less than 20% of the reported speedup on gradual shifts (Workload II) but substantially more on abrupt shifts (Workload I, B->D), measured as normalized average throughput and as time-to-restabilise after a phase boundary, compared with the paper's system.
addons.mechanism: Add a foreground counter that accumulates (r,u,p) per completed count window and exposes a smoothed estimate; feed that estimate to AdaptiveCompactionController::set_workload instead of the next window's ground-truth counts; replace remaining_window_cnt - today a lookup into a list of future change points precomputed over the whole trace - with an online hazard estimate (mean observed phase length, reset on change detection); extend need_reset_Mc so drift is detected on the workload tuple and not only on average run count; delete the hard-coded 'if (p > 0.9*(r+u+p)) { m=5; c=1000000; }' override; report oracle and online variants side by side so the gap is the measurement.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 4 (p.8) describes Workload Statistics as monitoring operations and reporting windowed (r,u,p) every 1M ops, and section 5.1 credits ArceKV with adapting 'within 20 million operations' (Figure 10(a)(b)). But the only paper-shaped harness in the repo hands the engine the true composition of the NEXT window before that window runs (tools/dynamic_test_util.h:431-467) and tells it exactly how many windows remain until the next shift (:473-479, derived from the change-point list built over the entire trace at :296-309). remaining_window_cnt is a first-class input to the cost integral - db/dyncompactioner.cc:152-156 clamps the simulation horizon to it - so it is not cosmetic. Additionally tools/dynamic_test_util.h:493-496 discards the simulation result entirely when point lookups exceed 90% of the mix (exactly sub-workload C, 98% point) and substitutes m=5, c=1000000, a hand-tuned constant that appears nowhere in the paper. Figure 9's table never separates 'adapted because it measured the change' from 'adapted because it was told'.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The estimator itself is small (~300-500 LOC) and local to two headers plus one call site. The cost is the harness: either resurrect tools/dynamic_test.cc (fix the FindBestMC namespace-lookup break at tools/dynamic_test_util.h:388,485, unpin the hard-coded /tmp/db at tools/dynamic_test.cc:144, stub reclaim_frag) or extend tools/arce_bench.cc with phase switching and an UPDATE opcode, plus write a Table-2 workload generator. All runs are CPU/NVMe only and fit at 1/5 scale on this machine, but the harness work makes this more than a localized change.
addons.research_value_rationale: It tests the validity of the paper's central claim rather than adding a feature: 'does a workload-driven compactor still win when it has to learn the workload?' is the first question a VLDB reviewer asks of any adaptive system, and the hard-coded p>0.9 override makes it sharper. Both outcomes teach something - a small gap robustly re-confirms the 2.17-2.92x headline, a large gap puts an asterisk on it - and the online estimator is a reusable artefact that the other add-ons can build on.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'ElasticLSM Arce compaction follow-up citing ArceKV 2026'; 'LSM-tree compaction online workload prediction change-point detection adaptive compaction 2026'; 'ArceKV workload-driven LSM compactions VLDB 2026 artifact'. No work citing ArceKV was found (arXiv 2508.03565 is Aug 2025, PVLDB 19(5) is 2026). Closest neighbours are Endure (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p1605-huynh.pdf), which tunes a static structure robustly under workload uncertainty offline, and SA-LSM (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2161-zhang.pdf), which uses survival analysis to detect workload properties for data layout rather than compaction scheduling. Neither audits an oracle assumption inside a score-based elastic compactor.

addons.name: range-overlap-aware-action-enumeration
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that extending ElasticLSM's candidate set with partial, key-range-scoped compactions - and charging them a cost proportional to overlapping bytes rather than whole-run bytes - reduces write amplification (compacted GB, Figure 9(b)) by at least 30% at equal or better read latency under skewed update workloads (YCSB-A/D Zipfian and the 1M-hot-key multi-version workload of section 5.3), compared with the paper's system.
addons.mechanism: ArceKV's three patterns are all whole-run: P1 takes the k smallest runs of a level, P2/P3 take ALL runs of levels i..j, and candidate cost is just the summed run size scaled by a constant. Key ranges are never consulted even though section 3.1 says a run carries a key range. Change: (1) carry per-run [smallest_key, largest_key] from RocksDB's FileMetaData into TreeState; (2) in EnumerateActions emit extra candidates restricted to a key sub-range, with compaction_size set to estimated overlapping bytes and the run-reduction reward discounted by the fraction of key space cleared; (3) extend apply_to_tree so the simulation models partial merges; (4) in the picker, translate a ranged action into CompactionInputFiles by intersecting with vstorage_->LevelFiles(i) rather than taking whole levels; (5) relax the 100 GiB output-file cap so a partial compaction can emit multiple SSTs.
addons.motivating_evidence: The cost model of section 3.2 (Eq 1-5) is a function only of the NUMBER of runs s and the BYTES X; key ranges enter nowhere, and the code confirms it - include/rocksdb/dyncompactionv4.h:147-156 scales every candidate's size by a flat rw_ratio/4096 with no overlap term. Section 5.2 'Space Amplification' reports ArceKV within 0.05 of Leveling only because 'lookup-driven compactions still merge overlapping runs', i.e. an incidental effect rather than a designed one, and Figure 9(b) shows ArceKV's compacted bytes are comparable to the eager baselines on Workload I - the flexibility buys latency, not write amplification. The released main branch makes this strictly worse: db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:404 caps output files at 100 GiB so every run is one SST, meaning a Pattern-2 compaction of a large level rewrites the entire level even when only a thin key band was updated - precisely the regime of section 5.3's MVCC case study and of YCSB-A/D.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Cross-cutting: it touches the state representation, the enumerator, the simulation's apply_to_tree, and the picker's file selection, and it grows the candidate set, so the pruning heuristics of sections 3.1/4 must be revisited to stay inside the claimed ~30 us decision budget. Still roughly 1-2k LOC confined to four files in one repo, with cheap CPU/NVMe evaluation on public YCSB traces, so it is well within a 10-week budget for 2-4 students - but it is not a localized single-module change.
addons.research_value_rationale: It attacks the paper's own simplifying assumption head-on: ElasticLSM is defined as 'a flexible collection of sorted runs, each tagged with a timestamp, size, and key range' yet the key range is never used in any cost or candidate decision. Key-range awareness is exactly how RocksDB's production picker avoids rewriting untouched data, so the comparison is meaningful to a storage reviewer. A negative result is equally instructive: it would establish that the run-count abstraction is sufficient and that range-aware enumeration does not pay for its decision cost.

scoop_check.details: Range-partitioned / overlap-aware compaction is standard in RocksDB's leveled picker and is studied in EcoTune, 'Rethinking The Compaction Policies in LSM-trees', SIGMOD 2025 (https://people.iiis.tsinghua.edu.cn/~huanchen/publications/ecotune-sigmod25.pdf), and splitting compaction tasks by overlapping key ranges appears in DownForce, ICPP 2025 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3754598.3754675). No work integrates key-range-scoped candidates into ArceKV's unconstrained, score-ranked action space under dynamic workloads, and nothing citing ArceKV was found (queries: 'ElasticLSM Arce compaction follow-up citing ArceKV 2026', 'LSM-tree concurrent parallel compaction scheduling multiple background workers cost model 2025').

addons.name: concurrent-compaction-action-sets
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that letting Arce select a SET of non-conflicting compactions for multiple background workers - and modelling worker occupancy explicitly in the short-term penalty instead of the current Amdahl fudge factor - improves throughput under 8-16 foreground threads (the regime of Figure 10(c)) by at least 25% over ArceKV with the same number of background workers, compared with the paper's system.
addons.mechanism: Today GetBestAction returns one DynAction and the picker bails out entirely (return nullptr) if ANY file in levels [start_level, output_level] is already being_compacted, so a second background worker is starved whenever the first is busy in overlapping levels. Change: (1) make EnumerateActions exclude in-flight runs and emit mutually disjoint candidates; (2) add a greedy set-selection pass that repeatedly takes the highest-scoring action disjoint from those already scheduled until workers are exhausted; (3) replace the 'parallel_factor > 1 => factor /= 2' heuristic (mirroring section 4's Amdahl phi = 0.5) with an explicit model of w workers and their aggregate I/O share; (4) fix the latent index mismatch between the being_compacted-filtered state built in GetCurrentStateForCompactedAction and the unfiltered LevelFiles indexing used when materialising the compaction.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 4's 'Multi-threading Extension' claims ArceKV 'tracks available compaction threads ... applying a large penalty when resources become saturated', but section 5 fixes the configuration to 'one background compaction thread and one flush thread', and Figure 10(c) states explicitly that 'the Moose framework does not support multiple background workers, so we fix the number of background threads to one and vary only the number of foreground query threads'. So the paper's own multi-worker mechanism is described but never evaluated. The code shows it is not merely unevaluated but structurally blocked: db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:383-387 returns nullptr for the whole decision if any file in the scanned level range is being compacted. On a 16-core machine with a fast NVMe a single compaction worker is the obvious bottleneck during write-heavy phase B, where the paper reports its largest win (10.60x).
addons.feasibility_rationale: The picker and scorer changes are contained (a few hundred LOC across three files), but evaluating the claim needs the multi-threaded harness ProcessWindowInParallel, which lives in the tools/dynamic_test.cc path that is excluded from the build and does not currently compile. Concurrency bugs in a modified RocksDB compaction picker are also a realistic time sink. Compute itself is cheap and entirely local to this machine.
addons.research_value_rationale: 'More compaction parallelism helps on a 16-core box' is a largely expected outcome and parallel/pipelined compaction has an established literature. The genuinely open question - whether the greedy single-action score stays near-optimal once several actions execute concurrently, i.e. whether the domination argument of Lemma 3.3 survives - is real but narrower in scope and less likely to change how the paper is read than the oracle or key-range questions.

scoop_check.details: DownForce, 'Revisiting Multi-threaded Compaction in LSM-trees: Enabling Compaction Pipelining', ICPP 2025 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3754598.3754675) pipelines and parallelises compaction tasks split by overlapping key ranges, overlapping with the mechanism but not with the question of multi-action selection inside a score-based elastic action space under dynamic workloads. Nothing citing ArceKV was found (query: 'LSM-tree concurrent parallel compaction scheduling multiple background workers cost model 2025').

addons.name: space-amplification-aware-effectiveness-score
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that adding a garbage-ratio term (duplicate plus tombstone bytes per run) to Arce's effectiveness score E(s,t,y) reduces peak space amplification by at least 20% on update- and delete-heavy dynamic workloads at less than 10% throughput loss, compared with the paper's system.
addons.mechanism: Eq 11 trades run-count reduction against read slowdown and stall penalty; nothing represents reclaimable bytes, and DynAction carries no notion of garbage. Change: (1) carry per-run num_entries, num_deletions and key-range overlap fraction into TreeState from RocksDB's FileMetaData, which already tracks them; (2) add a third term M_s * E_g(action) to get_reward_for_action where E_g estimates reclaimed bytes; (3) extend the FindBestMC grid with the new weight M_s (it currently searches only M in {5..95} crossed with c); (4) extend apply_to_tree so the simulated post-compaction run shrinks by the reclaimed bytes instead of being the plain sum of its inputs; (5) add a DELETE opcode to the benchmark and report DB size over time alongside latency.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 5.2 'Space Amplification' states outright that 'ArceKV focuses on read and write performance rather than space efficiency' and offers Figure 12(d) as a reassurance rather than a design goal - and the reassurance is measured on sub-workload J (uniform 33/33/33) while Table 2's A-J mixes contain no deletes at all. Section 5.3's MVCC case study is the one regime where garbage matters (1M hot keys over 100M operations) and the paper reports that ElasticLSM 'detects small incoming runs, assigns low compaction penalties (Equation 11), and converges to Leveling-like behavior' - i.e. it does the right thing by accident, not because the score knows about duplicates. A workload with explicit deletes, or a tight disk budget, is an unexplored regime where an engine that is free to defer compactions indefinitely (c can be set to 10^6, tools/dynamic_test_util.h:495) could plausibly do far worse than a structured LSM.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Fully localized: two engine files (db/dyncompactioner.cc, include/rocksdb/dyncompactionv4.h), the one place FileMetaData is read (db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:46-66), and a handful of lines in tools/arce_bench.cc - which is the harness that ALREADY builds - for the DELETE opcode and a size probe. FileMetaData already carries num_entries and num_deletions, so no new bookkeeping is needed in the storage engine. Well under 1-2k LOC, evaluable with the existing binary on this machine, and comfortably doable by 2-4 students in 10 weeks.
addons.research_value_rationale: Delete-aware compaction is well trodden (Lethe, SIGMOD 2020, introduced FADE/KiWi for exactly this), so the direction is expected and a reviewer would not be surprised that it works. What is new is putting a space term inside an unconstrained, score-ranked action space where the engine is explicitly permitted to defer compactions indefinitely - a strictly more dangerous setting than a fixed-structure LSM, and one the paper declines to study. Solid and well-scoped, but not a result that changes how the paper is read.

scoop_check.details: Lethe: A Tunable Delete-Aware LSM Engine, SIGMOD 2020 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3318464.3389757) covers delete persistence and space amplification for a fixed-structure LSM, and Scavenger+ (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.13935) revisits space-time tradeoffs for key-value separated LSM-trees. Neither addresses ElasticLSM's unconstrained action space or a score-based online compaction selector, and no work citing ArceKV was found (query: 'Lethe delete-aware LSM compaction space amplification tombstone persistence SIGMOD').

risks: Fidelity is the dominant risk: README.md:2 says in its first line that the main branch is a TikTok-specific in-memory adaptation that 'does not represent a faithful implementation of ArceKV'. Concretely the stall rate k is a compile-time constant (db/dyncompactioner.cc:5, kStallCost=4) so FindBestMC searches only (M,c) (db/dyncompactioner.cc:211-215) while the paper's Algorithm 1 searches (M,c,k); every compaction emits one 100 GiB-capped SST (db/compaction/compaction_picker_dynamic.cc:404); the simulation uses OpenMP, not the Eigen/SIMD vectorisation described in section 4. The dev branch is a third codebase with different class names (kCompactionStyleArce, ArceCompactionController) and a claude_md/ directory. Ask the authors which commit produced Figure 9 before committing the project.

tools/dynamic_test.cc - the only harness matching the paper's workloads, range lookups, cache/thread/threshold sweeps and Figure 13 case studies - is commented out of the build at tools/CMakeLists.txt:17 and almost certainly does not compile: tools/dynamic_test_util.h:388 and :485 call FindBestMC unqualified while it is declared in namespace DynamicLookForward (include/rocksdb/dynamic_lookforward.h:7-13) with no using directive and no ADL path from DynCompaction::TreeState. Budget repair time and treat 'we could not build the paper's harness' as a possible finding.

Oracle workload signal: the harness sets the compactioner's workload from the TRUE (r,u,p) counts of the next window (tools/dynamic_test_util.h:431-467) and derives remaining_window_cnt from a list of future change points precomputed over the whole trace (:473-479, :296-309), which feeds the cost integral at db/dyncompactioner.cc:152-156. If Figure 9 and Figure 10 were produced this way, 'adapts within 20M operations' measures the compaction engine, not the adaptation loop.

Hard-coded special case at tools/dynamic_test_util.h:493-496 replaces the simulation output with m=5, c=1000000 whenever point lookups exceed 90% of the mix - exactly sub-workload C (98% point). Any re-run must report results with and without this branch.

tools/dynamic_test_util.h:557 embeds a plaintext sudo password and shells out to 'sudo -S fstrim -v /tmp' every 10.24M ops (:503). Harmless on this machine (system() just fails and prints 'fail to trim'), but it should be reported to the authors, and it means the reference runs periodically TRIMmed the SSD between phases - a confound for long write-heavy runs that we cannot replicate.

grafite is an unconditional build dependency: table/block_based/filter_policy_internal.h:19 includes ../grafite/include/grafite/grafite.hpp with no guard and that header is pulled in across the table layer; .gitmodules uses an SSH URL; grafite itself nests lib/sux and lib/sdsl-lite. CMakeLists.txt:988-991 adds include directories but no link target, implying header-only use under -DSUCCINCT_LIB_SUX - unverified, and the most likely place the build stops. There is no configure switch to disable the range filter.

TBB is linked into every tool unconditionally (tools/CMakeLists.txt:26) while WITH_TBB defaults OFF (CMakeLists.txt:404), so a bare 'cmake ..' may fail to find -ltbb unless the conda prefix is on the link path; and FAIL_ON_WARNINGS defaults ON (CMakeLists.txt:356) on a RocksDB 9.5 fork built with gcc 12.2, so -DFAIL_ON_WARNINGS=OFF will very likely be needed.

Baseline coverage is incomplete by construction: Ruskey is not publicly released (paper footnote 2, p.8: 'obtained from the original authors'), so one of the eight Figure 9 rows cannot be reproduced; Moose/Tiering/LazyLeveling require the separate NTU-Siqiang-Group/MooseLSM repo and CAMAL a third repo. A faithful Figure 9 means building three codebases, not one.

DynAction::removed_files is a fixed 20x100 int matrix allocated per candidate (include/rocksdb/dyncompactionv4.h:19) and copied for every enumerated action; with c permitted to reach 10^6 the per-level run count can exceed 100, which is both a correctness hazard and an allocation cost inside the ~30 us decision budget claimed in section 3.1. Assert on these bounds in any scale-up experiment.

Disk headroom: full-scale Workload II (40 GiB preload + 94 GiB inserted, times ~1.2-1.4 space amplification per Figure 12(d), plus compaction transients) is uncomfortably close to the ~250 GB free on /home, especially since ArceKV is free to defer compactions. Use the 1/5 scale-down and monitor free space during runs.

Single-thread clock differs: the paper's i9-13900K boosts to 5.4 GHz while our Threadripper PRO 5955WX is a lower-clocked Zen 3 part, so absolute latencies will be higher. Only the ArceKV-vs-baseline ratios are meaningful - which is what Figure 9 reports anyway.

No artifact-evaluation badge was found for this paper (the ACM DL entry and the PVLDB PDF carry only an Artifact Availability statement), so there is no independent evidence that anyone outside the author group has rebuilt these results.
